name: Frost-assisted potato preservation
summary: Dried potatoes found at Quilcapampa, Peru, from about 835 to 900 CE are probably chuño, the frost-dried Andean potato that is light to carry and keeps for years.
description: Andean potato preservation using repeated exposure to frost and dehydration, producing a lightweight, durable dried food known as chuño. Present descriptions of the method do not establish every step for the earliest archaeological remains.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: High Andean nights bring hard frosts and the days are dry and sunny, so freezing and drying potatoes turned a perishable harvest into a stored food.

date.label: Approximately 835–900 CE
date.basis: The 2023 study gives the Quilcapampa occupation horizon as AD 835–900; this is the context of the material, not an invention or first-use interval.

events.statement: During the approximately 835–900 CE occupation of Quilcapampa, desiccated potatoes interpreted as likely chuño were present, and related starches were found in camelid dental calculus.
events.scope: Desiccated potato remains in a Middle Horizon settlement, interpreted by the study as likely chuño and assessed against modern starch reference morphology.
applications: Likely availability of preserved potato and possible camelid dietary exposure
events.population: People and herds associated with the Quilcapampa settlement
events.caveats: The Quilcapampa identification of the dried sample as chuño is probabilistic; the 2023 study sampled one desiccated potato, notes imperfect similarity for some granules, and its available text is a provider extraction. An exact preparation sequence at this site, whether a camelid was intentionally fed the product, its place of manufacture, and earlier origins are not established.

evidence.locator: Abstract and provider lines 625–629, 683–690, 695–709: methods, microbotanical results and discussion
evidence.supports: One desiccated archaeological potato and a dental granule were consistent with chuño; the authors date the Quilcapampa context to approximately 835–900 CE and infer that the product was available there.
Describes the traditional Andean alternating-freezing-and-dehydration process and its storage role.
